To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
pimozide changes response rates by directly acting on dopamine receptors and changes time perception through CRs.
pimozide produces behavioral-cognitive effects through both direct and conditioned actions.

the conditioned responses elicited by drug presentation may be responsible for changes in time perception and that this change in time perception may be a mechanism by which drug efficacy is increased.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the role of conditioned responses in the behavioral and cognitive effects of drugs of abuse.
the role of the CR in mediating drug action and with the mechanisms that underlie the development of CRs.

the behavioral and neural mechanisms underlying the development of drug tolerance, and we have found that the conditioned effects of drugs may play an important role in the development of this phenomenon.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
pimozide changes time perception through a conditioned response to stimuli that accompany drug administration.
the CRs eliciting effects of pimozide are not the same as the drug's direct effects.
pimozide produces a behavioral effect that is not mediated by its pharmacological action.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
dopamine antagonism can produce a conditioned effect on time perception.
the conditioned and unconditioned effects of a dopamine D-2 antagonist in rats can be dissociated.
the conditioned effects of drugs can be dissociated from their unconditioned effects, and the CRs eliciting conditioned drug effects can be dissociated in time from the drug's direct effects.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the behavioral-cognitive effects elicited by a drug may be mediated through different mechanisms.
the effects of drugs are not limited to the direct effects of the drug but also include the effects that the drug has on behavior and cognition.
CRs can be elicited by stimuli that accompany drug administration, and the CRs that are elicited may change the way that drugs are perceived.
